summary: Describes how a PIM multicast tree that crosses an MPLS network can be carried over multipoint LDP label switched paths. When a PIM Join arrives at the MPLS edge, information in it is used to set up the multipoint LSP, with no separate provisioning.

plainLanguage.summary: Multipoint LDP builds the paths that carry multicast traffic, but on its own it cannot say which packets belong on which path. This RFC puts the address of the multicast tree inside the label message itself, so the tree can be carried across an MPLS network without a second protocol to keep track of it.

questions: how does pim signal mpls multicast lsps
how does pim work over mpls
subtitle: How a PIM multicast tree can cross an MPLS network by hiding its source and group inside the mLDP label request itself.

tldr.problem: Multipoint LDP can build label switched paths that fan out to many receivers, but it never says which multicast packets should travel on which path. Without that mapping an operator needs a second, out-of-band signaling protocol such as PIM or BGP to tie the multicast trees to the MPLS paths.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC carries the identity of the multicast tree inside the mLDP message itself, in the opaque value field of the Forwarding Equivalence Class element. The root router of the path pulls the source and group back out of that field and hands them to its multicast code, which then continues with ordinary PIM processing.
tldr.outcome: The result is an IP multicast tree whose middle section is a multipoint LSP, spliced between IP multicast sub-trees on either side of the MPLS domain, with no extra signaling protocol. RFC 6826 is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 7438.

today: RFC 6826 is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 7438. It has not been obsoleted, and the mechanism it describes is still the way a PIM tree can be carried across an MPLS network without a second signaling protocol.

sections.title: The Missing Piece in Multipoint LDP
sections.content:
Multipoint LDP (mLDP) can build label switched paths (LSPs) that fan out to many destinations, and those paths are normally used to carry end-user multicast packets. What mLDP does not do is provide any rule for associating particular multicast packets with a particular LSP. Other documents, such as RFC 6513, describe deployments where an out-of-band signaling protocol like PIM or BGP establishes the mapping between an LSP and the multicast packets that should be forwarded over it.

This RFC removes that second protocol from the picture for one case. The information needed to establish the mapping is carried in the opaque value field of an mLDP FEC (Forwarding Equivalence Class) element. When an IP multicast tree enters the MPLS network, the (S,G) or (*,G) information from the IP multicast control plane is placed in that field. As the tree leaves the network, the information is extracted again and used to build the IP multicast control plane, and PIM messages can then be sent outside the MPLS domain.

The result is an IP multicast tree made of IP multicast sub-trees spliced together with a multipoint LSP. The RFC notes one asymmetry between the two protocols: PIM control messages are sent periodically, while the mLDP messages are not.

There is a cost to this design. Each IP multicast tree maps one to one to a P2MP or MP2MP LSP, so an operator should expect to see as many LSPs in the MPLS network as there are IP multicast trees, and should understand how IP multicast state is created so that it does not exceed the scalability numbers of the protocol, whether that is PIM or mLDP.
sections.plainLanguage: Multipoint LDP builds the paths for multicast traffic but does not say what should travel on them. This RFC writes the multicast tree's address into the path message, so no second protocol is needed to tie the two together. The trade-off is one path per multicast tree.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
Section 1.2 gives the document its vocabulary. A label switched path is a path through an MPLS network, set up by a label distribution protocol. A multipoint LSP, written MP LSP, is one of two kinds. A P2MP LSP has one ingress label switching router and one or more egress label switching routers. An MP2MP LSP connects a set of leaf nodes that may each independently act as an ingress or an egress.

An LSP is called a transit LSP when its FEC element contains the (S,G) or (*,G) that identifies a particular IP multicast distribution tree. The router at the source end is the ingress LSR, also called the root node; the routers at the far end are egress LSRs, also called leaf nodes. A transit LSR is a router with one or more directly connected downstream LSRs.

An IP multicast tree is identified by a multicast group address and, optionally, a source IP address. The pair is written (S,G) when the source is known and (*,G) when any source may be used. Two service models appear in the document. ASM is PIM Any Source Multicast, and SSM is PIM Source-Specific Multicast, where the receiver names the source it wants. A PIM Rendezvous Point (RP) is the router where receivers and sources meet in the PIM-SM model. In-band signaling, in this document, means using the opaque value of an mLDP FEC element to carry the (S,G) or (*,G) that identifies the tree.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC names its parts: the path that fans out, the router that starts it, the routers that end it, and the pair of addresses that identifies a multicast tree. A tree with a known source is written (S,G); a tree that accepts any source is written (*,G).

sections.title: In-Band Signaling for Multipoint LSPs
sections.content:
The worked example has IP-multicast-capable routers A and B on either side of an MPLS domain that contains label switching routers U, C and D. Router D is attached to a network that can do both MPLS multicast and IP multicast, and D is the router that has to create an IP multicast tree, because a PIM Join, an MSDP Source Announcement, a BGP Source Active auto-discovery route, or a Rendezvous Point discovery has told it that one is needed.

Suppose D can work out that the tree has to travel through the MPLS network until it reaches LSR U. Looking up the route to the source or the RP may show that the route is a BGP route whose next hop is U. D can then choose to set up a P2MP or an MP2MP LSP with U as the root, and make that LSP part of the IP multicast distribution tree.

To do that, D encodes a P2MP or MP2MP FEC element with the IP address of LSR U as the Root Node Address, and with the source and the group encoded into the opaque value. The RFC is strict about one point here: D MUST NOT use a particular opaque value type unless it knows, through provisioning or some other means outside the scope of this document, that U supports the root node procedures for that opaque value type. Which FEC element and opaque value are used depends on the IP address family, and on whether the tree is source-specific or bidirectional.

The handling rule is simple. An LSR that receives a label mapping or withdraw whose FEC element contains one of these opaque value types, and that is not the router named by the Root Node Address, follows the ordinary procedures of RFC 6388. The LSR that is the root extracts the multicast source and group and passes them to the multicast code. Processing a label mapping adds the downstream LDP neighbor to the outgoing list of the matching (S,G) or (*,G) state, creating that state if it does not already exist; processing a label withdraw removes the downstream LDP neighbor from that list. From that point on, normal PIM processing occurs.

One edge case is spelled out. If the LSR identified by the Root Node Address does not recognize the opaque value type, the multipoint LSP is still established, but the root will not send any multicast data packets on it.
sections.plainLanguage: The edge router that notices a new multicast tree builds a path across the MPLS network and writes the tree's address into the label message. The router at the far end pulls the address back out and tells its multicast code to treat the new neighbour as a normal PIM branch. Everything after that is ordinary PIM.

sections.title: What the Document Leaves Out
sections.content:
Several common cases are deliberately outside this document. A PIM shared tree, used by PIM-SM in the ASM service model, cannot be carried this way, because pruning an individual source from the shared tree would need an additional out-of-band signaling protocol such as PIM or BGP. Multicast groups that operate in PIM Dense-Mode are excluded, and so are source or RP addresses that are reachable in a VPN context.

The ASM service model is only partly covered. When PIM-SM runs in ASM mode, the usual way to discover active sources is to join a sparse-mode shared tree, and this document provides no method for establishing a sparse-mode shared tree across an MPLS network. Some other means of discovering the active sources is needed, and the RFC names two candidates: MSDP, and BGP Source Active auto-discovery routes. The choice is outside the scope of this document, and the RFC says so plainly: the document does not specify everything that is needed to support the ASM service model using in-band signaling.

For bidirectional trees the RFC assumes the RP is statically defined. It provides no procedures to discover RP-to-group mappings dynamically across an MPLS network, and puts dynamic RP mappings in combination with in-band signaling outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Some multicast setups are left out: shared trees that any source can feed, dense mode, and addresses inside VPNs. For the any-source case the RFC needs another way to find the active sources first, and it does not supply one.

sections.title: Source Trees and Bidirectional Trees
sections.content:
IP multicast source trees can be created by PIM running in either SSM mode or ASM mode. In SSM mode the source is known, so the tree is (S,G). In ASM mode the tree is (*,G) until a source is discovered, and the RFC requires some other mechanism, such as MSDP or BGP Source Active auto-discovery routes, to find active sources. Either way, the source and group addresses are encoded into a transit TLV.

A bidirectional IP multicast tree has no specific source address, so it MUST be transported using an MP2MP LSP. For a bidirectional tree the group address, the subnet mask and the RP are the parts that matter for multicast forwarding. The RP for the group is used to select the ingress LSR and the root of the LSP, and the group address is encoded according to the rules for the IP version in use.

There are two kinds of bidirectional state. The group-specific state is typically created when a PIM Join has been received, and it has a subnet mask of 32 for IPv4 and 128 for IPv6. The RP state is typically created through the static RP mapping and has a variable subnet mask; it is used to build a tree to the RP and is used for sender-only branches. Each state, group-specific or RP, results in a separate MP2MP LSP, and the merging of the two LSPs is done by PIM on the root LSR. No special procedures are necessary for that merge, because each LSP is effectively treated as a PIM-enabled interface.

Sender-only branches carry a warning. Packets for such a branch travel over an MP2MP LSP, and the other sender-only branches receive those packets as well. They will not forward them, because there are no receivers there, so the packets are dropped. If that effect is undesirable, some other means of transport has to be established to forward packets to the root of the tree, for example a multipoint-to-point LSP; the RFC points at a technique for unicasting packets to the root of a P2MP or MP2MP LSP.
sections.plainLanguage: A tree with one known source is carried over a path that fans out from one router. A bidirectional tree has no single source, so it uses a path where any leaf can be the source. That path needs two of its own, one for the group and one for the rendezvous point, and the router joins them up with its normal multicast code.

sections.title: The Four Transit TLV Encodings
sections.content:
The opaque value is not free-form. Four encodings are defined, one for each combination of IP version and tree type.

The Transit IPv4 Source TLV has type 3 and a length of 8 octets, holding an IPv4 multicast source address of 4 octets and an IPv4 multicast group address of 4 octets. The Transit IPv6 Source TLV has type 4 and a length of 32 octets, holding an IPv6 multicast source address of 16 octets and an IPv6 multicast group address of 16 octets.

The bidirectional variants carry the RP instead of a source. The Transit IPv4 Bidir TLV has type 5 and a length of 9 octets: one octet for the mask length, 4 octets for the IPv4 address of the RP used for the encoded group, and 4 octets for the group address. The mask length is the number of contiguous one bits that are left-justified and used as a mask, and its maximum allowed value is 32. The Transit IPv6 Bidir TLV has type 6 and a length of 33 octets, with the same three fields for IPv6: one octet of mask length whose maximum is 128, a 16-octet RP address, and a 16-octet group address.
sections.plainLanguage: The address pair is packed into a fixed format with a type number. An IPv4 pair takes 8 bytes and an IPv6 pair takes 32. The bidirectional versions swap the source address for the address of the rendezvous point and add one byte for the network mask length.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC has one sentence here. The same security considerations apply as for the base LDP specification, as described in RFC 5036.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC adds no security rules of its own. It points at the rules that already apply to the Label Distribution Protocol.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: Four values are allocated from the "LDP MP Opaque Value Element basic type" registry: Transit IPv4 Source TLV type 3, Transit IPv6 Source TLV type 4, Transit IPv4 Bidir TLV type 5, and Transit IPv6 Bidir TLV type 6.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps the list of recognised opaque value formats. This RFC adds the four formats it defines to that list, numbered 3, 4, 5 and 6.
